The complete issue and all ten comments were refreshed on October 11. Issue #13523 remains open and unchanged since October 2. The latest provider reply, from September 28, says a kernel-pinning execution property will be investigated; their preceding reply enabled the supported Linux 6.1 guest for the organization. No later comment announces a newer selectable kernel, documented pool or selection property. The three later comments are Tamir’s unanswered requests. This thread does not establish any new deployed kernel or backport state, so it supplies no basis to change current routing or credit a PTY fix.

Earlier diagnostic and request evidence, retained historically:

Fork-only PTY diagnostic source d192897ea1d6c4824a53e4b17cbe08485736d606 reproduces a byte-content failure in one of ten actual uncached native executions on root AMD64 Firecracker. At that point a conditional provider draft was prepared; the complete current issue thread contains no posted follow-up from that draft.

Earlier kernel and capacity evidence: Supported worker-kernel selection remains unresolved; issue #13523 is open with no new provider resolution. Source-only review of the retained failed core run finds ten non-FIB netfilter validation failures consistent with older Linux behavior and dual-stack native/hostnet reservation failures matching Linux fix d9ba9934285514f1f95d96326a82398a22dc77f2. Nine FIB cases retain an unresolved module/configuration boundary. All original outcomes remain FAILED; no new job, expectation weakening or source fix was introduced. Session-keyring expectations have a separately validated fix; PTY and timestamp failures remain unresolved. The user authorized the independently reviewed follow-up, and tamird posted it at 2026-10-02 13:44:22 UTC: https://github.com/buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy/issues/13523#issuecomment-5953753295. The exact published text was read back. Provider response and deployment remain pending; no worker with the requested settings has been tested. The original case assertion fails in 3 ms. This supports the address-index omission fixed by upstream Linux 936a192f9, while the deployed worker source and backports remain unknown. The user approved the additional follow-up, and tamird posted it at 2026-10-02 16:38:40 UTC: https://github.com/buildbuddy-io/buildbuddy/issues/13523#issuecomment-5956862042. The exact posted text was read back; provider response and deployment remain pending. No retry or qualification pass is claimed. The original IPv4 FIN_WAIT2 case passes in 5,001 ms without tuple snapshots, so the retained lookup differential is unresolved. No provider reply establishes deployment. Kernel coverage distinguishes documented Linux requirements from native syscall expectations. Actual October 2 AMD64 Firecracker workers report Linux 6.1.0 with the September 28 build identity and retained kernel notes; this is an observed worker, not an immutable selected kernel. Reports must retain actual kernel release/build and available configuration evidence with uncached results for each covered environment. Link?

> TestUIDMap in container_test appears to be failing.

Fixed in https://github.com/google/gvisor/pull/15920 and unrelated to this change, right? Can you please advance this one through the machine if you agree?

@EtiennePerot, I checked the failed import's complete diff against the
[public test log][1]. Both `TestUIDMap` failures occur in `New`, while boot
reads an [empty mount message from the gofer][2], before `Start`.

The test leaves `OOMScoreAdj` unset, and failed construction leaves
`c.Sandbox` nil, so cleanup also skips the OOM adjustment. The pidfd helper
extraction preserves the previous implementation. I found no changed
behavior on the failing startup path.

This is also different from #15920: the failed CI cases use a temporary
directory under `/home`, without that test's duplicate `/tmp` mount. The
underlying gofer failure remains unexplained because its log was not
uploaded; #15927 adds that capture.

Could you reconsider the changes-requested review on this PR?

nodes.status: Short pilot passed; full ping pair timed out
nodes.summary:
The complete ping pair timed out on both native host architectures at the original 300-second limits, in the first ICMPPortExhaustion case. Neither completed a case; 36 cases per owner were unstarted. Independent saved review bound both failures and the retained progress, without a speedup or cause claim. CPU attribution is being investigated separately. The earlier short mincore pilot remains a distinct two-host pass.

Earlier observations:

The paired mincore pilot passed both original 300-second actions, five cases on each native AMD64 and ARM64 OCI host. Independent review bound the 16 remotely inspected native tools, actual action inputs and byte-identical guest kernel, initramfs and payload. This short pair does not establish a speedup. The complete shared-filesystem ping pair is now accepted at eac536ce6 under its unchanged 300-second deadlines and full 37-case selection; its results are pending.

Earlier observations:

The resumed pilot passed graph routing and built both host archives, then its inspection step stopped on a BEP source-file path lookup before any TestRunner. The owner is preparing a narrow lookup correction; native-tool proof and guest execution remain unqualified. The source and guest choices are unchanged, and the partial evidence is being sealed.

Earlier observations:

The unchanged reviewed pilot resumed once at 588d3e6d3 after the pinned logical indexes became reachable again. Its original method, package checksum, exact-package fallback, two complete mincore targets and deadlines are unchanged. Results and native ARM64 host-tool proof remain pending; both prior zero-action failures are retained.

Earlier observations:

The reviewed source adds explicit ARM64-host tools for two existing complete mincore guests while preserving their payload, guest images and 300-second deadlines. Both pilot attempts stopped before execution. The first failed on the pinned AMD64 libexpat package. A single continuation used the standard Bazel exact-URL fallback; both official mirrors matched the existing package checksum. That continuation then failed when all four pinned jammy/main/amd64 package-index formats returned HTTP 503, before reaching the package fetch. There is no host-tool, ELF, placement, guest-runtime or timing result. Both saved failures are independently reviewed and retained. No further unchanged retry is planned while the immutable input prerequisite is unavailable. This fork pilot is not awaiting contributor review.

followup.disposition: Short pilot passed; full ping pair timed out
followup.nextAction: Use the separately authorized diagnostic evidence to investigate the retained timeout; do not promote the full host profile.

The KCOV tests assume every record is an instruction address in the top 2 GiB. gVisor records encode package, function and block identifiers, while Linux address layout varies by architecture and configuration. This proposal contains the portable assertions and obsolete-constant removal; the qualification harness instrumentation remains separate. items.body:
[🤖] 1 issue found:

- **[minor · concurrency]** Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race (`Makefile:269`, inline)

[🤖] **[minor · concurrency] Re-enabled metric_test flakes under CPU load from profiling restart race**

This change makes all three `make unit-tests` CI jobs run `//pkg/metric:metric_test`, but `TestMetricProfiling` fails intermittently when the CPU is busy, as it is during `make unit-tests`. `writeProfilingMetrics` (`pkg/metric/profiling_metric.go:645-647`) signals `doneProfilingMetrics` before it clears `profilingMetricsStarted`, so `StopProfilingMetrics` can return while the flag is still set. The next subtest's `StartProfilingMetrics` then fails with "profiling metrics have already been started". The race predates this PR and does not depend on the architecture; the exclusion removed here kept it out of CI.

**Suggested fix:** Fix the race before removing the exclusion, or keep `-//pkg/metric:metric_test` until it is fixed. In `writeProfilingMetrics`, capture the channel when the goroutine starts and clear the flag before signaling:

```go
func writeProfilingMetrics[...](...) {
	done := doneProfilingMetrics
	...
	sink.Close()
	profilingMetricsStarted.Store(false)
	done <- stats
	close(done)
}
```

Capturing `done` is required: with a plain reorder, the next `StartProfilingMetrics` reassigns the global while the old writer still uses it. The race detector then reports a race between lines 287 and 647, and runs panic with "send on closed channel" (100/100 runs failed). Verified: with the fix, 0 failures in 1,100 loaded runs and 220 race-detector runs.

<details><summary>Details (evidence, reproduction and test code)</summary>

**Evidence:** `StopProfilingMetrics` returns right after it receives from `doneProfilingMetrics` (line 748). `StartProfilingMetrics` needs `profilingMetricsStarted.CompareAndSwap(false, true)` (line 264). If the writer goroutine is descheduled between the send and `Store(false)`, a Start that follows Stop fails.

Results of `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=N` on a 32-core amd64 host ("paired" means PR head and head+fix ran at the same time):
- 32 parallel runs (bazel default): head 4/200 failed.
- Paired, 32 parallel runs each: head 32/400 and 14/400; fix 0/400 and 0/400.
- `--config=race`: head 9/40 and 20/80; fix 0/40 and 0/80 (the 80-run pair ran concurrently). No DATA RACE reports.

Every failure is `metric_test.go:1228: StartProfilingMetrics error: got 'profiling metrics have already been started'`, spread over six subtests. Runs pass when executed one at a time on an idle machine.

`TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop` (attached) restarts profiling 200 times right after `StopProfilingMetrics`. Paired under load, it failed 110/300 runs at head and 0/300 runs (60,000 restarts) with the fix.

The original #10045 failure is fixed: an ARM64 build of the test under qemu-aarch64 passes at head and fails with "did not panic" when the IsNaN check is removed.

**Reproduced with a test** (`pkg/metric/metric_test.go`): `bazel test //pkg/metric:metric_test --nocache_test_results --runs_per_test=300 --test_output=summary   (run concurrently with: <same command>; slot fix = worktree + scratch/max/fix.patch). Earlier runs used --runs_per_test=200/400 (existing TestMetricProfiling only) and --config=race --runs_per_test=40/80.` → Fails intermittently on the PR head under parallel load, always with 'profiling metrics have already been started'. Passes every run with the fix applied under the same concurrent load.

**Test code:**

```diff
diff --git a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
index cb33abdd9..9f0a3586a 100644
--- a/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
+++ b/pkg/metric/metric_test.go
@@ -1430,3 +1430,34 @@ func TestMetricProfiling(t *testing.T) {
 		})
 	}
 }
+
+// TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop checks that StartProfilingMetrics
+// succeeds as soon as StopProfilingMetrics returns.
+func TestProfilingMetricsRestartAfterStop(t *testing.T) {
+	defer resetTest()
+	if _, err := NewUint64Metric("/foo", Uint64Metadata{
+		Cumulative:  true,
+		Sync:        true,
+		Description: fooDescription,
+	}); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("NewUint64Metric: %v", err)
+	}
+	if err := Initialize(); err != nil {
+		t.Fatalf("Initialize: %v", err)
+	}
+	dir := t.TempDir()
+	for i := 0; i < 200; i++ {
+		f, err := os.CreateTemp(dir, "profiling-metrics")
+		if err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("CreateTemp: %v", err)
+		}
+		if err := StartProfilingMetrics(ProfilingMetricsOptions[*os.File]{
+			Sink:    f,
+			Metrics: "/foo",
+			Rate:    time.Millisecond,
+		}); err != nil {
+			t.Fatalf("iteration %d: StartProfilingMetrics: %v", i, err)
+		}
+		StopProfilingMetrics()
+	}
+}
```

</details>

Stop now clears the started flag after receiving the writer’s final statistics. The send is the writer’s last access to the channel, so an immediate restart can safely replace it. Fixed in a52b53673b4b5d9585685592d9c188197bb7f520.

Posted by Codex on behalf of @tamird.

nodes.head: 7ae55f4cc07eb541c8d63442a343a3c2564dfd6f
nodes.title: tcp: ACK window overruns while FIN is unread
nodes.summary:
The contributor approved exact closing-window correction 7ae55f4cc07eb541c8d63442a343a3c2564dfd6f for upstream opening after #16377 lands. That fixture landing is the sole remaining delivery gate; no contributor decision remains pending. After a peer FIN, payload crossing the advertised right edge receives the current cumulative ACK while FIN or queued data remains unread. Peeking preserves the unread state. A consuming EOF read, or reading the final queued byte before a separate EOF read, ends these probe responses. The test keeps CLOSE_WAIT and observes absence of ACKs for one second. Both runs apply source-verified patches to the hosted qualification base; neither is a direct build of the public fork tree.

nodes.summary:
The approved e396b8c8a proposal is delivered as #16419 at d13561b12 with an identical diff. No contributor decision remains pending. Current public checks and maintainer review are tracked on the PR.

A ten-segment flight set the slow-start threshold to five segments with Reno and seven with CUBIC on the first timeout. When the same retransmission timed out again, the sender reduced the threshold to two. The published change preserves five or seven until a timeout reaches new data, as RFC 5681 requires. In separate tests with no ACK and a half-segment ACK, the old code failed four cases per run; both corrected runs passed all 13 cases. These tests cover repeated timeouts on the same bytes; #16393 reported advancing oldest data.

Broader validation passed 536 records across TCP, race, packet and analyzer checks, with one existing RACK skip. All seven packet cases passed. Each analyzer passed for AMD64 and ARM64; the runtime checks were on AMD64.

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, test-only change that does what it says:

1. The `CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE` drop is the right fix for `TestCreateController`. `generic_permission()` would otherwise let a privileged worker create the subdirectory under the 0555 parent. The only cleanups that run afterwards are owner-permitted `chmod` and `RemoveAll`, so they keep working.
2. The extracted `capabilitytest.DropEffective` keeps the old thread-safety properties and makes the failure path simpler: the modified thread is always discarded instead of being restored on a best-effort basis.
3. I checked the remaining `runsc/cgroup` tests, and none of them need a host cgroup mount or D-Bus, so removing `local` looks safe.
4. Optional nit: mention in the package doc that importing `capabilitytest` locks main to the initial thread through `init()`.

The PR merges cleanly into current master.

---
[🤖] This review is part of an experimental auto-review process to help speed up gVisor review velocity. It is a work in progress. Assisted-by: Claude

Optional nit: since importing this package changes the whole test binary (main is locked to the initial thread in `init()`), it may be worth saying so in the package doc, e.g. "Importing this package reserves the initial thread for main."

I added this to the [package comment](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/35532f26ad7a54dcbcf6484d7adf451978976726): importing `capabilitytest` locks the main goroutine to the initial OS thread so tests can discard threads whose capabilities they change. The edit is in a separate cleanup so this PR can finish importing.

items.body:
LGTM. This is a small, correct change:

1. The `+checklocks:epollMu` annotation covers every access to `FileDescription.epolls`. `Release`, `addInterest`, `DeleteInterest` and `DecRef` all hold `epollMu`, and the generated stateify methods are already `+checklocksignore`.
2. The new `DecRef` comment explains the detach-then-unlock pattern correctly, and it matches the lock order documented in `vfs.go`.
3. Optional nit: mention that this mirrors Linux's `eventpoll_release_file()`, which also drops `file->f_lock` before taking `ep->mtx`.

The PR is based on a recent master and neither touched file has changed since, so I expect no conflicts.

---

Optional nit: you could point to the Linux analogue here, e.g. "...takes interestMu before epollMu. This mirrors Linux's eventpoll_release_file(), which drops file->f_lock before taking ep->mtx."

I added the Linux comparison in [the cleanup](https://github.com/tamird/gvisor/commit/35532f26ad7a54dcbcf6484d7adf451978976726). [`eventpoll_release_file()`](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/adc218676eef25575469234709c2d87185ca223a/fs/eventpoll.c#L1095-L1107) drops `file->f_lock` before taking `ep->mtx`, the same lock ordering as in `DecRef`. nodes.head: 3257b4b2a6481c604f656db18c74456b0355f38b
nodes.title: Wake signalfd waiters when the signal mask changes
nodes.summary: Published at the approved 3257b4b2a6 as #16598. If a blocked signal is already pending, changing a signalfd mask to include it makes the fd readable. On stock gVisor, epoll registered under the old mask missed this transition for two signal variants even though read returned the pending signal. Notify waiters after updating the mask and releasing the lock. Linux and the corrected systrap passed both variants and both existing poll controls; the signalfd Nogo owner passed for AMD64 and ARM64. The combined run remains failed because its two stock negative cases failed as expected.

nodes.head: 2a7fbd97ab07a3df881e6e20b9613a3b613796c8
nodes.title: Compare RACK timestamps across a clock wrap
nodes.summary: Published at the approved 2a7fbd97ab as #16600. RACK compares a peer’s echoed TCP timestamp with the time a segment was retransmitted. When the 32-bit counter wraps, stock RACK records a 5 ms RTT from an older echo and ignores a later echo that should produce a 5 ms sample. Use the existing serial-number comparison. All 45 TCP tests passed on each native architecture, and both owning Nogo checks passed for AMD64 and ARM64. This changes RTT attribution; the test does not measure throughput.

evidence.label: Fork: RACK comparison and both clock-wrap cases
Stock AMD64: both wrap cases fail
TCP and test Nogo: both target architectures passed
Original paired run: FAIL on the stock cases

nodes.head: 978bcdf025e2226dff0c3cbfb4554c2f0b9ea853
nodes.title: Require a TCP timestamp echo for Eifel detection
nodes.summary: Published at the approved 978bcdf025 as #16601. After an RTO, the stock sender counted a timestamp-free ACK as evidence of spurious recovery. Both counters increased to one even though the post-ACK flag was clear. The fix requires negotiated timestamps and a timestamp option on this ACK. With the same partial ACK, both counters stayed zero without timestamps and reached one with a valid echo. The complete TCP SACK wire suite passed 31 cases each on native AMD64 and ARM64. This tests recovery detection, not throughput.

Library and wire-test Nogo: AMD64 and ARM64 passed
Original comparison FAIL: stock counters differed, but the verifier also expected the post-ACK flag to differ

contributorReview.head: 55210b651ecb1c5350d8011c0997669f392f8870
contributorReview.title: Build both release architectures with an explicit version
contributorReview.summary: Build both release architectures from one caller-supplied label without Git or the status script in the Bazel checkout. Both Debian controls reported 20261029.0; eight binaries per architecture matched across the Debian and both tar packages.
contributorReview.body:
Release packaging currently asks Git to identify the checkout. A source
export falls back to 0.0.0, so two different exports can report the
same version. Let the release caller provide one label to both
architecture builds. Runsc, its sidecars and the result parser use that
label; the Debian version strips the prefix as before.

The default checkout still supplies its Git revision or release tag. A
custom status command that sets STABLE_VERSION keeps precedence. Builds
with no identity no longer accept a checkpoint or sidecar solely because
the two missing values are equal. The historical 0.0.0 fallback remains
available to ordinary builds; an explicit release cannot use it.

Built real AMD64 and ARM64 Debian packages and both release archives
with neither the source tree's .git nor its status script available.
Both Debian controls reported 20261029.0, and the eight ELF files on
each architecture matched across all three package formats. On AMD64,
runsc restored a checkpoint of its own release; a different revision
rejected the checkpoint and the mismatched Sentry rejected startup.

The first workflow is red: its inspection image lacked the zstd CLI,
and its summary mishandled a Bazel event. A read of all six original
output digests verified the packages without repeating a build or
restore. This does not change changelog timestamps, release signing, or
publication.

investigations.title: CUBIC recovery and congestion-control testing
investigations.summary: The reporter’s original stall has a tested repair. Separately, gVisor enlarged its post-loss congestion window on writes that never filled it. The candidate keeps its window stable across three write schedules; Linux kept its window stable in all four sparse-write flows.

findings.text: The current-master control failed the small-flight slow-start cases: a ten-segment window grew to 11 after one outstanding segment and to 15 after five. The corrected sender passed those cases and the 10→20→40 continuously backlogged rounds. Its CUBIC first burst was 14 and its Reno first burst 12 with or without the spaced writes. A Linux comparison remains outstanding.

In an independent SACK recovery test, the oldest 500-byte hole was retransmitted after only 1.5 s despite a 3 s RTO. A later covering ACK arrived after the old deadline. With two holes, restarting the timer on the successful repair of the oldest hole gives it a full RTO; repairing the later hole does not postpone it. All 92 corrected TCP/SACK/RACK cases passed. This timer bug does not account for the previously measured queue delay in the sparse-loss Reno run.

evidence.label: Stock 1.5-second retransmission under a three-second timeout
Stock with both holes repaired: timed out early
Corrected TCP, SACK and RACK suites: 92 passed, no skips
Two analyzer outputs pass for AMD64/ARM64; parent verifier did not join individual worker XMLs

findings.text: Both algorithms first repaired the same 1,420-byte range at the same time. Reno had built a larger queue; its timer fired before the ACK for that repair could return. CUBIC repaired the range without a timeout. This explains a divergence in this fixture, not a general CUBIC advantage or the cause of the reported outage.

evidence.label: Native test and original packet traces

findings.text: On the same 10 Mbit/s finite queue, the manual clock and Go synctest produced identical packet and stream traces in both CUBIC/Reno write orders. CUBIC writing first produced 12,405 events and 119 drops; Reno writing first produced 12,430 events and 98 drops. Both clocks agreed on which flow sent first at 250 ms, on every drop and scheduled delivery, and on each flow's delivered bytes. This was one trial per clock and order on one native AMD64 worker at GOMAXPROCS=1. Automated verification took 7.9 seconds from execution finish.

evidence.label: Four native runs and their packet traces

findings.text: Two established TCP flows shared one NIC. Across eight runs, each write order produced the same ten packets at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 2. Writing the second flow first reversed both the data at 60 ms and the ACKs at 70 ms. Both payloads (20 and 30 bytes) arrived once; neither flow retransmitted during two RTOs. This tests simultaneous readiness, not competition for a full queue.

evidence.label: Comparable finite queue with both clock drivers (fixture, awaiting results)

findings.text: After dropping the second of five 1,420-byte segments, the virtual link recorded three acknowledgments with growing SACK blocks. Reno and CUBIC each retransmitted just the missing segment after 20 ms, before the 200 ms retransmission timer. The receiver delivered all 7,100 bytes exactly once; each sender counted one fast retransmit, one SACK recovery and zero timeouts. All eight runs (two algorithms, one or two processors, two trials) reproduced the same 14 packets. During recovery Reno’s window fell from 10 segments to 5; CUBIC’s stayed at 10 at that sample. This measures a single connection recovering from one loss. The trace does not establish a throughput advantage or distinguish the effect of the SACK information from that of duplicate ACKs.

evidence.label: Original packet traces and TCP counters
Two-stack link, deliberate loss and assertions

findings.text: Two real gVisor TCP stacks reproduced the same packet schedule for one connection over a link with a 10 ms delay each way. The client sent 33 bytes at virtual time 30 ms. With no loss, the server acknowledged them at 40 ms; the sender recorded no timeout or retransmission. When the fixture dropped that segment, no packet or data appeared one nanosecond before the 200 ms timeout. At 230 ms the sender retransmitted the same sequence and payload; at 240 ms the server acknowledged all 33 bytes. The sender counted one timeout and one retransmission, and the receiver read the data only once. Both modes produced identical TCP headers, payloads and times across two trials each at GOMAXPROCS=1 and 2. The fixture pauses dispatchers and checks each expected packet before advancing time. This covers a single flow with tail-loss probes disabled; it does not establish that several flows drain in a deterministic order. An earlier fixture sent an already-parsed buffer to the receiver and stopped before the handshake completed.

evidence.label: Two-stack wire and retransmission traces on Linux AMD64
Fork fixture with the link, timeout and delivery checks
Earlier fixture stopped after the initial SYN

findings.text: A real TCP endpoint retransmitted an unanswered SYN after 1.0003 seconds on the Linux worker. Under plain Go 1.27.3 synctest, the SYN was sent but Wait stayed blocked until the five-second watchdog: the idle TCP processor was parked in Sleeper.Fetch. Pausing the single stack once let Wait return without advancing time. No retransmission was queued one nanosecond before the RTO; the same SYN appeared at exactly one virtual second (4.1 ms wall time for the child). This proves a handshake timer can run while the dispatcher is paused. It does not establish a deterministic two-stack link simulator.

evidence.label: Real SYN, plain bubble and paused stack: native worker result

findings.text:
The sustained two-sender FIFO experiment confirms the earlier first-write sensitivity over longer virtual-time windows. CUBIC delivery decreases, while Reno consumes previously idle link service. The first-write-order difference in CUBIC delivery share narrows from 42.3473 to 1.94965 percentage points. All finite flows drain, but total accepted work differs because demand ends at the same virtual time; drain duration is not a fixed-work timing comparison. Native finish to automatic verification was 11.972167 seconds. This scoped evidence does not establish CPU cost, native throughput, general fairness or a recommendation to change the default algorithm.

findings.text: The fork-only read-boundary control on b6b0ffbcb6 ran the same packet probes against native Linux 6.18.57 and unchanged netstack. Within the one-second probe observation, native Linux sends the unchanged ACK for unread FIN-only probes and both peek cases; exact-size and oversized consuming reads suppress that ACK in both combined and separately ACKed wire arrangements. Netstack suppresses all probe ACKs. All six added cases per backend preserve the expected data, EOF and TCP state. The original two netstack failures plus their parent remain: three remote uncached owners produce 16 positive and three failed XML records, so aggregate FAIL is preserved. Separately ACKed wire packets do not prove distinct receive skbs, and these observations establish no general read-budget requirement. Root owns the queued-window compatibility repair. Corrected invocation 81663166-f6db-40fe-b73e-736ea9c028b3 at c6d9e691a8c667f9cca4330b0bb8f1a3dc5d2656 has an authenticated inner PASS: four owners, 24 positive XML records, inner native/capture/runner exits zero and no missing cases or errors. Independent wire review checks all ten packet cases per backend, including five required ACK and five no-ACK observations, with positive data/EOF/state assertions. The original consumer receipt correctly remains FAIL. The same invocation’s retained outer terminal log now identifies the post-test failure: after the four native tests and producer passed, the bootstrap diagnostic-size guard raised ValueError: Bootstrap diagnostic stream exceeds 8 MiB bound. The outer command exited 1 at 2026-10-24 21:38:39.948 UTC, and the original archive was uploaded successfully. This resolves the outer failure without changing the focused native/source/wire evidence into a successful overall qualification; no test replay or aggregate PASS is claimed. This work is separate from the reviewed EOF279e and future-ACK3d17 proposals.

findings.text:
Historical focused TCP evidence, now filed with the TCP investigation. The two independently approved fixes were subsequently delivered as #16377 (EOF fixture) and #16378 (future ACK); unread-FIN/queued-window compatibility remains separate.

The owning testbench analyzer and both canonical format checks add three positives: seven remote uncached attempts, 63 total positive records, no failures or skips. Reject ESTABLISHED segments that acknowledge unsent data before delivering their payload or passing their acknowledgment to the sender, and send an unchanged acknowledgment through the existing limiter. The shared test checks that rejected payload is not delivered and valid traffic can continue. Public-base proposal 3d17e956611c17719835876ac9d1d63c4c85a38e was later delivered as #16378, with no prerequisite PR. The test-only baseline d517 retains native FAIL and proves both invalid payload deliveries; corrected 245c passes native Linux and netstack plus TCP Nogo and goimports (four remote uncached owners, 16 positive XML records). This focused result does not cover FIN-specific rejection, limiter saturation or performance.

The EOF result validates explicit empty-queue fixture setup. Root separately owns unread-FIN/queued-data compatibility: the original right-edge payload has no in-window byte, and the observed Linux control acknowledged and discarded it while the current gVisor closing path silently dropped it. Linux 9ca48 introduced the nonempty-queue/end-sequence check; partially overlapping payload is a separate policy question. findings.text: A retransmission timeout interrupted SACK recovery on a controlled Reno connection. The first subsequent ACK covered only 2,848 of 17,088 outstanding bytes. The baseline sender then started fast recovery three times before the outstanding flight had been acknowledged. Preventing those repeat entries let the transfer finish in 0.771 seconds with one timeout, compared with 2.090 seconds and three timeouts. Changing only the reordering timer had no effect in this experiment; it never fired during timeout recovery. With the separate flight-accounting proposal applied, the same change reduced completion time from 0.807 to 0.723 seconds, although the original recovery boundary was reached later (309 vs. 289 ms). Each variant gave identical packet traces in two attempts. These are simulated connection times for this loss pattern; they do not reproduce the Windows incident in #16393. The first calibration generated sparse SACKs but never timed out; its failed qualification is retained.

findings.text: In a paired Reno/CUBIC run, the first loss occurred at 664.2976 ms on both source revisions: a 1,472-byte frame added to 123,648 queued bytes exceeded the 125,000-byte FIFO. Adding room for one frame admitted those same bytes and moved the loss to a later segment. Disabling HyStart left the first loss, repair and covering ACK unchanged. Three packets had been selectively acknowledged before fast recovery repaired the hole; no timeout occurred before the cumulative ACK. The traces on either side of the SACK fix matched through that ACK. This rules out the first loss as the point where the later timeout counts diverge in this scenario.

The two senders matched through 2,256 packet events and the same Reno timeout at 1.772693134 s. After a partial ACK, both declared 75 segments lost. Stock Reno re-entered SACK recovery for the same flight, cut its threshold from 38 to 2 packets, sent one repair, and timed out on the next packet. The corrected sender sent both repairs and took no second timeout. Restoring just the old recovery-entry conditions reproduced all 4,186 stock packet events, including five timeouts versus one. This identifies the effect of #16495 in this scenario; it does not establish a CUBIC default.

On a 20 Mbit/s link with 150 ms RTT and a deep loss-free queue, Reno, CUBIC, and CUBIC with only ACK-train detection disabled delivered all 5,021 frames at identical times and lengths (7,124,996 bytes). The link stayed busy from 753 ms. HyStart exited at 829 ms; disabling its ACK-train detector increased the peak queue from 191,360 to 236,992 bytes and the final smoothed RTT from 175.887 to 213.595 ms. On this path the early exit reduced queueing without reducing delivery.

In congestion avoidance with the same 64 one-segment writes and ACKs, CUBIC sent 17 segments in the next backlogged flight with no application gaps and 29 with 90 ms gaps. Reno sent 16 in both. With neither sparse phase, CUBIC sent 14 and Reno sent 12. No later loss or timeout occurred, and the receive window was identical. These are observed bursts, not a throughput or fairness result.

After recovery below the initial window, stock gVisor CUBIC sent [7, 8, 8, 9, 9] segments across five backlogged flights without a gap, versus [7, 10, 15, 23, 34] after 30 seconds idle. Reno sent [7, 8, 9, 10, 11] in both cases. On Linux 6.18.57, after a full congestion-avoidance flight, the idle interval did not change either reported congestion window or five-flight byte total. In both algorithms one new segment left one ACK earlier. No measured flight experienced a retransmission or timeout. These measurements do not identify the cause of the historic customer outage.

findings.text: In four independent packet traces, thirty seconds idle inflated stock CUBIC’s fifth backlogged flight from 9 to 34 segments before its first full congestion-avoidance flight, and from 10 to 40 after it. The pending window-use change preserved both five-flight sequences with or without the idle interval: [7, 8, 8, 9, 9] and [8, 8, 9, 9, 10]. Reno was unchanged in both controls. The narrower experiment that added an idle timestamp to every sender is unnecessary.

Reselecting CUBIC reset gVisor’s window from 7 packets to 10 after loss. Switching after a peer FIN changed the option name but left the old sender active. Linux and corrected gVisor preserve the window and use the selected controller for the next loss. A switch to Reno with 21 credits and a 10-packet window now grows to 11, keeping the new ACK as one credit.

investigations.title: pkg/state: code generation and generics design
investigations.summary: We are helping review the maintainers' graph codec. The integrated encoder can save two views of one Go map that its decoder refuses to restore; the review on #16584 includes a reproducer and a tested fix. Our separate interface-setter experiment stays closed: it made GraphLoad slower and added allocations.

findings.text: For one live byte in Parth’s graph writer, increasing capacity from 1 B to 64 KiB to 16 MiB changed the wire from 42 to 46 to 48 B, but the address-index slot and entry buffers from 1,072 B to 14,336 B to 3,039,224 B. At half load, inserting a different object in the same block kept 32 keys but doubled slots 64→128. These are Save index capacities, not whole-heap or timing results.

Set byte 7 to 0xa7 or 0xc9, shorten an eight-byte slice to length 1, and checkpoint it. Both codecs restore zero at byte 7 after reslicing; only legacy overwrites the caller’s byte during Save. With a second, full-length view visited after the short one, the integrated graph restores the marker and the two views still share storage; legacy clears the marker. The public graph tip’s private writer produced marker-dependent streams only with the full view; its graph Load is not wired up.

evidence.label: Legacy round trip and exact public graph writer

findings.text: Both string-storage policies restored five tasks from the same 163,712-byte Nginx state file. The kernel frame contained 1,152 small strings totaling 12,289 bytes; both policies allocated one 16,384-byte slab. The CPUID frame used no slab. The smaller policy saved space on the two-byte fixture, but neither this checkpoint nor the 20,000-node graph saved a slab. No speed or heap gain was measured.

evidence.label: Nginx checkpoint and native execution log

findings.text: Both restore strategies passed the graph identity checks. For a 22-byte checkpoint with one 2-byte string, bounding the decoder slab reduced backing capacity from 16,384 to 2 bytes. On the seeded 20,000-node graph both strategies reserved exactly 1,490,944 bytes in 91 slabs for the same 145,654 small strings. This measures buffer capacity; it does not establish a heap or speed improvement.

Two overlapping named slices of pointers round-trip in both traversal orders. Converting one to a pointer to a three-element array in safe Go makes Save reject both orders on the integrated rewrite. The control and both failures use the same backing array.

evidence.label: Control and both failing traversal orders

findings.text: The integrated graph encoder rejected two partially overlapping slices of three-byte elements only when it discovered the lower-address window first. The unsigned address difference wrapped before the element-alignment test; reversing order and four-byte controls passed. Comparing the two address residues fixed the round trip: both overlapping positions retain pointer identity and writes are visible through the other restored view. The split #16584 source contains the same expression but was not executed.

Inline review with reproducer, addressed to Parth

findings.text: Two fields can share one Go map after a legal conversion to a named map type. Running the identical test on three sources showed that the legacy codec rejects it during Save; the integrated graph rewrite reports a successful Save, then rejects its own stream at Load. Comparing the key and element types on both paths lets the two views share one restored map without conflating an independent third map. All same-type controls passed on each source.

All 11 hook subcases passed; on both sources, two loads from the same slot restored 7 and each destination’s hook observed [7]. In 12 paired runs against stock (bd7e3d2a8a), GraphLoad was slower in 11 pairs and allocated more in all 12. Neither the map nor plain-struct timing difference was significant (p=.932 and p=.347). The decoder prototype now finishes a value before copying it into a map or interface, and tracks pending writes only for structs that actually have them. This fixes the observed map-key and shared-slice restore bugs. Loading the same wire slot into two destinations also runs each hook exactly once on the right value. On 1,024 ordinary structs, stock and candidate both used 5,702 allocations in every sample; bytes fell 11.90%. The graph fixture still used 3.45% more allocations and 1.80% more bytes. The full normal and race suites passed (10,798 and 10,844 cases respectively; each retained 87 skips), as did the three analyzer targets on AMD64 and ARM64. In twelve paired AMD64 samples, plain struct Load took 557.9 vs. 556.0 µs (p=.478). The map fixture used 12.99% fewer bytes and six more allocations per operation. No whole-checkpoint or startup measurement was made.

findings.text: A handwritten StateSave that saves the same child in two slots restored one shared pointer on the parent (79 bytes) and two distinct pointers on the encode-dedup experiment (83 bytes). findings.text:
Formatting the finalized state statistics lazily, once per log message, avoids the eager table rendering when no output consumes it. The 120 samples reuse one genuine finalized kernel Save/Load Stats input. Encoding happened outside sampling and sink writes were in memory. This measures formatting CPU/allocation cost, not physical logging, checkpoint I/O, actual restore or whole startup. The separate naive deferred-pointer control rendered twice with two outputs; the per-message memoized helper removes that duplication. The source-bound prototype and independently reviewed retained result passed; no new contributor decision or competing state rewrite is proposed. Parth retains rewrite ownership.

The current generator emits Save/Load calls with addresses of statically known fields. Sink.Save and Source.Load then accept any and reconstruct reflect.Values. The prototype will retain that known type information in generated field operations while sharing the existing wire/type/identity/wait graph. AST spelling alone is insufficient for imported, aliased or shadowed types; the generator needs a sound type proof or a compatible dynamic fallback.

At the studied Go 1.27.1 pin, the specification and compiler support generic methods. Array lengths still require constant expressions, and generic code is not automatically devirtualized. Language feasibility therefore does not establish an allocation or timing benefit.

Pointer identity, cycles, interior aliases, overlapping slices and delayed load callbacks must retain their semantics under one graph mechanism. Those requirements do not make reflective field traversal unavoidable: generated descriptors and typed operations can carry known representation information. The prototype must preserve registration before reentrant hooks and distinct aggregate storage where callbacks retain addresses; compatibility for arbitrary dynamic types remains part of the design.

The initial prototype specializes proved scalar/pointer fields and uses typed allocation and assignment while retaining the same wire and object-identity/wait graph. Pointer identity metadata still traverses the current reflective boundary. A later descriptor-based encoder could discover and snapshot objects once, then emit finalized IDs without boxing every wire value; it must cache hook/SaveValue results and captured values because callbacks and slice-tail clearing can mutate state. This is a design direction, not an executed performance result.

findings.text: Etienne’s zero-size field experiment skips StateSave and StateLoad when the Go type occupies no bytes. A source audit of 116 types owning state hooks or custom conversions at the experiment’s parent found no zero-sized production type with observable hooks. There is an API compatibility question for external implementations: a zero-sized SaverLoader can save a value derived from context or arrange an AfterLoad callback, and those operations would be skipped when it is stored as a field. This was a source review; it did not reproduce an in-tree runtime regression.

The proposed decoder allocates a 16 KiB backing array on its first short string. A fork-only experiment compares that size to the bytes remaining in the stream while decoding exactly the same input. It verifies the restored string and graph identity. The kernel experiment measures state.Load on a checkpoint; it does not resume nginx tasks. Results pending.

Six fresh processes restored the same five-task Nginx kernel in 5.72 ms cold and 1.22 ms warm (medians). In a separate instrumented arm, object value decoding took 4.61 ms and 0.67 ms. The first restore spent 1.53 ms of that decoding phase building metadata for 1,132 types; the second had no slow-path calls. These are measurements of the integrated graph implementation, beyond public PR #16584.

evidence.label: Native graph restore from an Nginx checkpoint
Original reports and verified phase measurements

findings.text: On the first restore of a 164,150-byte Nginx checkpoint, 1,132 type records were constructed during kernel value decoding. Of these, 541 were used only as pointer wrappers for slot arguments, 500 were used elsewhere in decoding, 34 were consulted only for layout checks during construction, and 57 had no observed lookup. The second restore built no new types. The counts describe this fixture; they do not measure the time saved by deferring any group.

evidence.label: Two native restores and four counting windows

findings.text: Avoiding the intermediate pointer-type record did not produce a useful improvement on a pristine 164,393-byte Nginx checkpoint. Across 16 alternating pairs, the median candidate-minus-control change was +5.322 ms from launch through first successful restore (candidate faster in 5/16), -0.093 ms for the first CPUID and kernel loads (9/16), and -0.006 ms for the second loads (8/16). All 64 restores completed with matching tasks and features. The original reporter confused the Bazel launcher PID with its child; recovery verified the original outputs without rerunning. No product change is proposed.

evidence.label: All 16 original pairs and source identity
Original run with failed launcher-PID assertion

findings.text: 208 fresh children completed 416 restores of the same Nginx checkpoint. Of 388 CPU samples, 113 fell under the cold kernel state.Load and 43 under the warm load. The allocation profile attributed 474,736 bytes and 13 allocations per restore to growth of the decoder’s callback list. The profiling bracket forces garbage collection, which can evict the decoder’s reusable storage; this does not establish the allocation cost of an ordinary warm restore.

evidence.label: Cold, warm and blank profile measurements

findings.text: A capped callback-buffer reservation saved a median 310,688 bytes and 11 allocations across eight cold Nginx restores; warm allocation counts and bytes were unchanged. In 16 paired timings, the first kernel load was 0.354 ms faster by median difference, but startup through the verified restore was 0.308 ms slower and only 7 of 16 pairs were faster. The reservation is not proposed. Of the 1,725 enqueued kernel callbacks, 1,016 are dependency edges, 531 are AfterLoad hooks, and 178 are LoadValue callbacks; immediately executed callbacks are excluded.

Storing callback dependencies in a more compact FIFO saved 260,632 bytes per cold Nginx restore across eight paired allocation samples, but used 12 more allocations. Across 16 paired timings, first verified kernel load was 6.386 ms faster by median difference; only 9 of 16 pairs improved and the differences ranged from 182 ms faster to 428 ms slower. The hook-heavy fixture grew from 31,654 to 33,355 B/op and 6 to 7 allocs/op. There is no established startup improvement, and this is not proposed for the rewrite. The wrapper failed because ordinary Go benchmark output has no individual PASS record: each original benchmark log contains all 32 iterations and a successful exit; the unit-test records passed.

evidence.label: Native Nginx startup and callback measurements
Original wrapper failure and retained evidence

findings.text: On Parth’s patch-16 decoder components, a direct interface and a pointer-to-value both kept the hook’s pointer; an interface copied into a map kept nil although the hook ran once. Delaying insertion fixed the direct key and two-map cases too. This is a component test; this head has no public graph Load dispatcher.

Spare slice capacity did not dominate the index when saving one real Nginx kernel. Three successive Save/Load rounds restored five tasks and wrote 2,036 kernel objects in 148,453 / 148,458 / 148,461-byte frames. Only 15 of 1,051 / 1,038 / 1,048 distinct 512-byte blocks were covered exclusively by spare capacity; these accounted for 15 of 2,748 / 2,744 / 2,761 index entries. The CPUID root had none. These counts do not measure elapsed time or predict safe savings.

evidence.label: Original test log, XML and counts

findings.text: On the integrated graph serializer, an Nginx kernel Save averaged 1.578 ms and 1.93 MB allocated across 1,742 iterations. The exact 148,247-byte checkpoint reloaded. Of sampled allocations during Save, 5.62 MB of 17.38 MB went to object-record storage, compared with 1.18 MB to each address index. These are allocation-profile totals, not per-operation counts. The native test passed; its workflow rejected the worker metadata, and the original profiles were recovered by digest without re-execution.

investigations.nextStep: Measure how much spare slice capacity contributes to the address index during the existing Nginx kernel checkpoint. Also check that the integrated graph loader exposes a repaired map entry to its parent’s AfterLoad.

investigations.title: pkg/state: reflection CPU and allocation profiles
investigations.summary:
The recorded profiling and fixed comparisons are complete. Their mixed and negative results remain below; the subsequent decoded-frame qualification and architecture experiments continue in the separate state design investigation. This profiling record has no pending execution or contributor decision.

The completed pointer experiments remain unpromoted: the first coherent-pointer comparison had five timing regressions, two gains and twelve nonsignificant results; the enclosing-pointer comparison had three regressions, four gains and twelve nonsignificant results. Earlier helper, map-registration and reader experiments remain separate evidence.

The generated restore successor is now implemented and independently correctness-qualified. It uses one authoritative graph pointer and a static restoration callback, shared map/array ordering, typed destination operations and exact registered-type callback selection. Four corrected full suites plus eighteen retained owners and two production links pass; thirteen serialized streams match across four groups. Original shared-fixture construction failures remain recorded. Runtime-sized slice backing retains the existing reflection boundary.

Its fixed comparison is mixed and unpromoted: five Load timing gains, two adoption slowdowns and twelve nonsignificant timings across 52 actions and 456 rows. Load allocations fall, while the state and UDP test executables grow 19.54% and 25.48%. The separate RestoreEmpty pilot passes all six save/load iterations, with overlapping Load ranges and a 21.50% larger runsc; three CPUID-warmed operations per arm are descriptive, not a significance or cold-start result.

A separate two-line shared-envelope consolidation at b941f2f056 passes six owners and four matched executable checks. It reduces runsc by 1,634,304 bytes on AMD64 and 1,507,328 bytes on ARM64 relative to the measured successor. Timing was not rerun, so this size result does not remove the earlier performance limitations. A further shared-struct helper at 2831e4a8e2 passes six owners and three groups of thirteen matching streams. Its matched executables shrink again relative to b941: runsc by 1,814,528 bytes on AMD64 and 1,507,328 bytes on ARM64. The subsequent fixed shared-struct comparison is independently closed and still mixed: nine timing gains, three regressions and seven nonsignificant results. Focused captured/uncaptured adoption profiles are also closed. Array restoration occupies 42.58% and 46.08% cumulative CPU in the candidate profiles, including nested restoration, statistics and waits; those overlapping sampled totals do not identify reflection alone as the cause or predict a speedup. No successor is proposed for adoption.

The runtime-array revision at e0515a1d8b has a fully reviewed fixed comparison against coherent control 225fdf9301. It shows five Load timing gains, a 3.54% UDP Save regression (p=.039), and thirteen nonsignificant timings. Captured and uncaptured adoption Load medians rise 2.62% and 3.45%, respectively, without statistical significance; that does not establish equivalence. The state and UDP test executables grow 50.24% and 59.79%. This revision remains unpromoted.

The shared array-loop/view revision at 173993df1f passed six test/analyzer owners and three groups of thirteen matching streams. Its state and UDP test executables are 8,573,088 and 8,994,976 bytes, down 5.42% and 5.87% from e051. Its original production-link deadline is retained separately from the completed link continuation. The subsequent shared-pointer helper at fffd29842d6d passed the focused correctness checks and production links. Its runsc executables are 54,141,088 bytes on AMD64 and 50,790,560 bytes on ARM64. The AMD64 executable remains 37.23% larger than the retained coherent control (39,452,832 bytes); the production comparison has a recorded version-stamp input difference and is not a byte-attribution or startup claim.

The shared-pointer fixed comparison 8ae794ca is independently closed: seven timing gains, five regressions and seven nonsignificant results. Captured and uncaptured adoption Load regress 4.60% and 6.91%; state and UDP test executables remain 38.29% and 46.16% larger than the matched coherent control. This mixed result remains unpromoted.

The earlier shared-pointer idle-Nginx restore pilot remains independently confirmed incomplete: each arm produced two one-iteration observations, then the third restore failed during Docker/containerd checkpoint upload. The four observed rows do not complete the required six-row pilot. Native exit status, BEP and parent status incorrectly reported success despite benchmark failure text and XML failures; the original discrepancy is retained. It supplies no complete end-to-end comparison or adoption claim.

The data-plan successor at 221124de7 is independently correctness-qualified. Its fixed comparison has seven timing regressions, one gain and eleven nonsignificant results, and remains unpromoted. State/UDP test executables grow 2.64%/2.81%; matched runsc files grow 2.41% on AMD64 and 2.48% on ARM64. Reviewed diagnostic profiles identify per-Load metadata construction and recurring dispatch/parsing costs without proving causal effect sizes. A separate Nginx pilot completes three actual restores per arm; overlapping small-sample timings do not establish a performance improvement.

The metadata-ownership revision at 5401bbaba is independently qualified for the selected correctness and race checks, with three groups of thirteen streams matching the prior data-plan source. Single measured-Load allocation reductions are observed, alongside increased initialization allocation counts. The adoption fixture uses Save-only setup, but ControlMessageDecoding performs an untimed validation Load before measurement; its row is not a first-use layout cost. Each timing has only one observation, so these measurements do not establish a timing improvement. Production executable sizes are unchanged from 221124de7 and remain about 2.4% larger than the coherent control. The candidate remains unpromoted.

The fixed idle-Nginx comparison of metadata-ownership source 5401bbaba against coherent control 3aa3a761c is independently closed: all twenty-four actual checkpoint-and-restore operations completed, twelve per arm, each starting a fresh sentry. Median observed time rises from 0.876 seconds to 1.157 seconds (31.98%). The measurement includes restore and port-presence detection, not HTTP readiness or populated traffic. Repetitions share one worker per arm, so worker effects remain uncontrolled and the difference cannot be attributed solely to code. The candidate remains unpromoted.

The narrower owner-lookup revision at e444abe2e is independently closed for ten fresh correctness/analyzer owners and single measured-Load cost checks. The control-message observation uses 96 more bytes with the same 102 allocations after an untimed validation Load; it is not a first-use layout cost. Initialization totals are unchanged. Test executable file lengths are unchanged, with text sections 192 bytes larger. Single measured-load observations and the closed diagnostic profiles do not establish a latency improvement; the candidate remains experimental and unpromoted.

The byte-reader comparison is independently closed. On the deterministic synthetic pointer/slice graph through the real uncompressed statefile reader, twelve fixed balanced pairs show no detected time benefit (median 766,202.5 to 760,387 ns, p=.198), 16 additional bytes per operation and unchanged 4,953 allocations per operation. All twenty-six native processes exited successfully, with twenty-four measured rows; the original parent failure and XML reporter errors remain recorded. These saved measurements were authenticated without rerunning benchmarks. This is not a whole-kernel restore or fresh-sentry startup measurement. The byte-reader revision remains unpromoted.

The decoded-frame architecture uses one parser and generated restoration methods. Both stable-block and inline candidates remain unadopted. The simpler contiguous revision passes correctness and its fixed comparison: large synthetic Load is 19.00% faster with 36.85% fewer allocated bytes, while control-message timing has no detected change. Executable file sizes are unchanged. Independent review is complete. The completed 24-operation whole-restore comparison does not establish an overall speedup. Subsequent profiling and the unsuccessful type-description sharing experiment are recorded in the design investigation; no successor has been adopted.

findings.text: Map reflection was the strongest measured reflection opportunity. In sampled allocation-object profiles, reflect.unsafe_New accounted for 51.12% flat in Map Load and 25.41% flat in Map Save. Map Save also spent 25.13% cumulative CPU in MapKeys and 15.24% in MapIndex; cumulative entries overlap and must not be added.

Other costs would survive simply replacing reflective field access: Stats.sample accounted for 21.24% cumulative CPU in Pointer Load, while the 32-packet UDP Save profile attributed 40.06% of sampled allocation objects to wire.Struct.Alloc and 26.53% to encodeStruct. Sample percentages are estimates, not exact allocation counts or predicted savings.

All five profiling actions completed, but the original parent failed because its collector expected a ZIP. The ten individual CPU/heap files were retained and decoded in a tool-only continuation, with no benchmark repetition. The original failed parent remains failed.

Independent saved-result review verified all 192 measured rows, 12 balanced AB/BA pairs and the actual source-to-binary inputs. Map Save medians were 240.95 versus 214.75 ns per normalized unit (benchstat −10.87%, p=.020, 12 samples per side); allocated bytes were 156 versus 129 (−17.31%). None of the seven other timing comparisons was statistically significant in this run; this does not establish equivalence. The production difference is only the delivered MapRange loop.

Source review withdrew the first one-line decoder preallocation candidate before testing. Normal referenced maps are eagerly allocated in decodeObject before decodeMap, so adding a size hint only in decodeMap misses the owning allocation path. No preallocation measurements were run; the next candidate must address the actual map-creation path.

evidence.label: Decoder allocation ownership in the measured cohort

findings.text: The struct/header coallocation experiment changes only encode.go and wire.go against the fixed-work baseline. Independent review verified 264 measured rows and 12 balanced before/after pairs per cohort. Control-message Save uses 11.76% fewer allocations; UDP queue Save uses 12.83%, 19.03% and 20.30% fewer at 1, 8 and 32 packets. All eleven timing comparisons are nonsignificant (smallest p=.060). Allocated bytes are essentially unchanged and serialized sizes are identical. This remains an experiment, not a ready PR or checkpoint-speedup claim.

Reusing decoder temporary key/value slots outside Struct and Array kinds reduced the fixed 1024-entry Map Load median from 449,457 to 368,672 ns (-17.97%, benchstat p<.001, n=12). Allocated bytes fell 6.71% and allocations fell 52.47%. Root verified the original 192 measured rows and 12 pairs. Only decode.go differs between the measured inputs; the seven other timing comparisons were nonsignificant.

Reusing scalar iterator storage reduced the separate fixed 1024-entry Map Save median from 195,068 to 184,478.5 ns (-5.43%, benchstat p=.010, n=12). Allocated bytes fell 6.17% and allocations fell 35.82%; seven other timing comparisons were nonsignificant. The original measured rows and numeric interpretation are independently reviewed. MapRange #15542 subsequently landed, and the contributor-approved iterator-storage change is delivered as PR #15621.

The shared-primitive prototype at 74c23e08a passed the selected five-owner compatibility scope. In the paired study, pointer Load improved by 7.72% (p=.002); the other eight timing changes were not significant, and allocation counts did not change. findings.text: The first direct framed prototype is public at b83596347, with qualification e0292b990. Its per-arm wire size is 12,873 bytes and allocation count is 3,623, unchanged within that repeat; the earlier integration cohort used different absolute values.

The separate checkpoint compatibility pilot passed six restore operations, but three operations per arm with the same reported executor-worker ID do not establish a timing effect or identical VM/CPU placement. The closed allocation profiles identify piece growth and per-struct capture storage as added costs. They are process-wide sampled estimates, not exact per-operation allocation accounting. investigations.title: Scheduled tracker refresh reliability
investigations.summary: The active default-branch workflow requests ten-minute refreshes, but the latest twenty scheduled events remain hours apart. A scheduled event resumed at 20:12:49 UTC on 22 October after the prior 15:39:50 event, passed and published the 20:14:12 snapshot. This does not explain the gap or establish regular cadence. The separately requested refresh 39845533696 passed 104 tests; its optional batched mergeability recheck received HTTP 502 and retained UNKNOWN observations while the strict reminder conflict guard remained in force.

findings.text: At the 11 October schedule audit, the default-branch workflow was configured for minutes 18 and 48 of each UTC hour. The latest scheduled run observed by that audit was created at 01:01:30 UTC on 11 October and completed the 01:03:14 snapshot in status-only commit 560dd0edb. That newer automated snapshot was preserved before the curated update. Five earlier scheduled runs succeeded on 10 October, created at 01:18, 07:45, 13:59, 18:39 and 22:00 UTC. Successful execution is established, but the observed multi-hour gaps before event creation do not demonstrate regular 30-minute cadence. Their cause remains unexplained.

The configuration and run-history audit found no disabled workflow, wrong default branch, blocked job or queued run explaining the gap. The missing events occur before job execution, so there is no failed job log identifying their cause. No replacement scheduler or repeated re-registration has been introduced.

GitHub documents that scheduled jobs can be delayed or dropped. That is a service limitation, not proof of this gap’s cause. Manual publication through the existing collector is keeping verified snapshots visible while regular automatic cadence remains unproven.

The October 15 scheduled refresh collected successfully but lost a publication race to a metadata update. Workflow acffb2cb5 now recollects on the latest site revision after a confirmed concurrent update. The validation run reproduced that race and published on its second attempt; Pages deployed the new snapshot while preserving the README update. Authentication or transport failure against an unchanged remote head still fails the job.

The request-limit failure came from repeatedly fetching terminal source and import history. The corrected collector uses a complete open-PR inventory to discover reopening, confirms closures of previously active records, and refreshes known active imports even under terminal sources. Thirty Python regression cases run before snapshot collection in Actions. The successful live run used 20 requests and preserved 131 terminal-source observation clocks; historical terminal details do not acquire a fresh timestamp.

The enabled workflow on the actual default branch schedules minutes 18 and 48 each UTC hour. The 17 October audit found no newer scheduled event after the successful 00:31 run through 03:29 UTC, despite valid configuration and no queued or disabled job. The official-Ruby HTTP migration remains agent work because the native-gem tools are not yet portable through the ordinary Make image path. All complete Entry values remained unchanged. Six native phases exited zero; no tests, HTTP consumers or image assemblies were rerun. This validates the candidate catalog against the existing policy, without adopting the candidate records or changing policy.

The original public audit 289a3144 remains FAIL: eight preparation/build phases passed, including both CPU native-gem outputs and both image archives, but Fetch and Verify each rejected ten singleton license lists before doing their work. The correction changed those lists to the scalar form required by the public checker. Its focused recovery d321c46b was verified 3.98 seconds after native completion. The original public archive and native tar/profile identities matched the earlier qualified outputs; their source-specific image evidence remains valid independently of the original catalog failure.

The source-bound fork experiment on 86b8d128d5d5 passed the unchanged TestRuby HTTP consumer under AMD64 runc and systrap, plus the inspector for both CPU archives and native-extension ABI. The earlier repeatability result covers the two architecture-specific gem payloads. ARM64 Docker execution remains unqualified.

Portability still requires a complete declared C compiler, make, sysroot, target Ruby ABI and matching execution-CPU contract. The examined portable Ruby headers match 190 non-generated headers per CPU, but its static Ruby/OpenSSL configuration differs from the qualified official image; header similarity alone does not establish extension compatibility. Keep the working public Dockerfile and do not present a Ruby contributor proposal yet.

Earlier source-specific Ruby consumer and supplier assessment:

The existing Ruby HTTP consumer now passes on remote AMD64 workers under both native runc and gVisor systrap. On source 6e2a86620241, both TestRuby cases loaded the same archive (2d55be5414b2) and image config (4af0598eae31), then passed the HTTP 200 and Hello World assertions. Source 7ff366cdbb0a applies only that emitted formatting, and the separate 8befae51 singleton buildifier run passes. The consumers were not rerun. This closes the existing Ruby image consumer gap, not an image migration, ARM runtime, performance or reproducible-image claim; the recipe still installs unpinned Sinatra, rackup and Puma dependencies.

A source-only assessment of rules_img packaging for the unchanged Ruby HTTP server found no small drop-in native-gem supplier. rules_ruby v1.0.0-rc2 supplies pinned gem fetching, offline bundle installation and exportable gem files, but native extension compilation inherits its compiler from PATH and does not bind the native-extension outputs to the image’s Ruby ABI and target CPU. The inspected current Puma 8.0.2 and nio4r 2.7.5 gem archives contain extconf.rb and no prebuilt shared objects; these inspected versions are not asserted to be the historical image’s installed versions. A usable supplier must declare the native compiler, target Ruby ABI and AMD64/ARM64 outputs. No migration source, dependency change or new runtime qualification follows from this assessment.

investigations.summary:
Two production observations explicitly deferred from #13781 remain uninvestigated and outside the fixture correction: a disappearing-file NotFound can abort the startup WalkDir before later files enter the LRU, and Close does not wait for the startup scan, which may still mutate files after shutdown synchronization or boot_id removal. These are recorded findings, not newly authorized fixes or established causes of the current Windows timeout.

investigations.title: Build on scratch workers with no undeclared tools
investigations.summary: Remove the builder image from the supported build. A clean worker must be able to build from declared Bazel toolchains and inputs, including any shell, interpreter, system libraries or helper programs an action uses. Move Make recipes into Bazel where that removes an undeclared dependency; eliminating all Makefiles is optional.

findings.text: Building //:release directly on the hosted Ubuntu runner failed because an AMD64 build tried to compile the ARM64 systrap stub. Selecting only the target architecture for normal Go builds fixed the failure: the same runner completed 3,994 Bazel actions without the Docker builder and uploaded the same eight paths as upstream. Both systrap sources remained in the configured //:gopath graph. The twelve generated files in upstream’s Go branch provide an exact-source comparison for the exported ZIP.

evidence.label: Direct Bazel release and three graph checks
Upstream Go export of the control source

findings.text: A single build produced both architectures’ Debian, bzip2 and zstd packages: six outputs, totaling 399,083,591 bytes. Each digest was traced to an uncached packaging action and staging action on the empty worker. The Actions wrapper failed afterward on a cquery option. The public //:release binary directory is a separate target: its GitHub upload must be checked separately. Reconciliation on the original artifacts resolved the cquery alias and passed the source-image audit. The GitHub workflow then reproduced another dependency: an AMD64 release invoked /usr/bin/aarch64-linux-gnu-gcc to build the ARM64 systrap stub and failed because the runner has no cross compiler.

The combined empty-worker release reached //test/release:artifacts and failed: source genrules invoked /bin/bash, the Go standard-library build required /tmp, and PackageTar used a Bash launcher. Its single-target verdict was available 0.253 s after the Bazel command returned. Separately invoking the declared Python directly for PackageTar and MakeDeb produced byte-identical tar and .deb artifacts on empty AMD64 and ordinary AMD64/ARM64 workers. That attempt did not produce the full set of release packages.

evidence.label: Combined release on scratch: target failed; complete verifier receipt
PackageTar and MakeDeb on ordinary and empty workers

findings.text: The Go bootstrap ran on the empty AMD64 worker with a declared ash executable, the original Go SDK and a writable temporary directory. The two outputs matched the independently built Python control byte-for-byte. Without the temporary directory, the Go tool failed before compilation. The supplier change depends on rules_shell exposing the shell executable as an action input.

rules_python 2.4.5 removes two shell actions that generated constant build metadata for the tar and Debian writers. The writers produced identical packages on ordinary AMD64 and ARM64 workers. On an empty worker the metadata was generated, then both package launchers failed to execute.

evidence.label: Empty worker reached the package launchers

findings.text: The AMD64 compiler-rt builtins target now builds on the pinned scratch worker. Explicitly selecting musl for execution platforms changed the 7,368-byte helper linked to the host ELF loader into a 44,296-byte generator. Its CppModuleMap action executed remotely without a cache hit on the same image. Execution finished at 00:43:42.675 UTC and the passing verdict appeared at 00:43:42.983; review of the single bundle confirmed the physical execution. This did not change target-platform libc or qualify the full release.

evidence.label: Generator could not start on the same scratch image

findings.text: Giving compiler-rt a writable temporary directory eliminated the Clang temporary-file diagnostics in the isolated AMD64 build. It still failed: the only failed action was the supplier’s CppModuleMap helper. The OCI executor could not start the staged native module-map-generator; the executable’s exact missing dependency remains to be identified. The 233 remote processes are not a successful full target.

The complete six-archive release target failed on the same physical shell-free worker where the copy control passed. The action log identifies five failure types: Bash-based gVisor version and seccomp genrules, rules_python build metadata, rules_go bootstrap, the Protobuf toolchain version check, and Clang assembly intermediates on an image without /tmp. The seccomp generator already has PR #16590. Clang alone accounted for 139 compiler action errors in the log; a focused compiler-rt run tests a writable action-local temporary directory. The source is the fork integration branch, not current master. No archive success is claimed. Native execution finished at 23:06:04.789 UTC; the invocation verdict was available at 23:06:05.048 (+0.259 s), and the complete row at 23:06:05.344 (+0.555 s). Reading the action log to identify the five causes was the remaining manual work.

The pause image passed a filesystem inventory but had ENTRYPOINT /pause on AMD64 and ARM64. BuildBuddy’s OCI runner prepends that entrypoint to the requested action. The first control was cancelled and retained a failed verdict with no executed row. The replacement is a digest-pinned hello-world image: both Linux roots contain only /hello and have no ENTRYPOINT. Its default CMD does not override Bazel’s executable. The replacement executed the CopyFile action remotely with no cached result; Bazel reported two internal actions and exactly one remote action. Its profile recorded 6.179 s for CopyFile. The row finished at 23:00:52.000 UTC; a verified verdict followed at 23:00:52.223 UTC.

findings.text: An existing rules_python ZIP plus a declared interpreter reproduced the stock tar.gz, .deb and .changes bytes in a strict empty root. On default supplier toolchains, creating the two ZIPs took 19.859 s and 22.496 s, and each ZIP was 81.6 MB. Both packaging variants passed 40/41 default tests and failed the same preserved-file-mode assertion. The reported 255 MB per ZIP is the sum of uncompressed members, not a measurement of bytes unpacked per invocation.

investigations.title: O_TMPFILE on immutable procfs directories
investigations.summary: With the gofer path-walk change from #15773 and the immutable-directory check from #16473, gVisor returns EPERM like Linux when O_TMPFILE | O_RDWR targets /proc/self or /proc/thread-self. This closes the observed errno difference on writable procfs.

findings.text: The comparison added only the seven-line gofer change from #15773 (bd3f9073e4) to the tested #16473 revision (eb15b3a970). Linux, systrap with directfs, and systrap in shared mode all returned EPERM for both directories, by absolute path and relative to an O_PATH descriptor for /proc, with CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE both effective and dropped (24 calls). #16473 alone already returned EPERM for the eight descriptor-relative guest calls. Its earlier absolute-path controls returned EOPNOTSUPP in both guest modes and EPERM on Linux; those controls did not explicitly vary the capability. These results concern the rejection of writes to immutable directories, not whether anonymous-file creation works on other filesystems.

Both changes: native Linux and both systrap modes
#16473 alone: calls relative to the proc directory

findings.text: In the tested gofer-root configuration, gofer rejects O_TMPFILE before walking into /proc. Open #15773 defers gofer’s unsupported-operation check until the dentry is resolved; #16473 supplies the immutable-directory write check. The earlier runs tested the ordinary procfs change without that path-walk correction, not the two changes together.

investigations.title: TCP performance reports and independent PR reviews
investigations.summary: Track TCP reports and proposed fixes across gVisor and the downstreams that supply packet traces. Separate recovery after loss, low-RTT timers, receive pressure, offload and application-visible latency.
investigations.nextStep: Monitor replies and revised heads on #16659 and #16660. Test receive pressure and corked shutdown separately from loss recovery. Include new issues and external PRs in the TCP review pass.

findings.text: Initial census: 510 open PRs inspected by changed path and title, including exports. The networking/performance labels and TCP, retransmission, SACK, RACK, CUBIC and netstack searches yielded 184 distinct candidate issues; many are not TCP defects.

A downstream reporter observed that #16081, #15432 or #16495 individually prevented their no-timestamp synthetic stall in the configurations they tried. #16081 preserves RTO recovery across duplicate ACKs; #16495 preserves the boundary specifically after an RTO interrupts SACK recovery. #15432 updates the estimate of packets still in flight, a different mechanism. The production path and kernel settings remain unconfirmed.

Two independent authors’ timer proposals address different bounds: #15785 adds a multi-packet delay on very short RTT paths; #15972 caps the probe deadline at the retransmission deadline. Review them together under idle, no-ACK and delayed-ACK conditions. The timestamp and new-data probe changes need separate tests for incomplete SACK ranges and invalid ACK numbers.

Outside burst loss: #14092/#14101 report excess packets in flight after benign reordering; #14102/#14458 address undoing congestion response after spurious recovery. #15144/#15325 concern receive-buffer pressure, and #14011/#14579 concern forwarding large packets. #15253 is a downstream offload report, not yet established as the same forwarding defect. #16437 reports a 200 ms close/shutdown delay with TCP_CORK, independently of congestion control.

On #16659, RACK advanced to byte 40 for both a SACK of the entire retransmitted [30,40) segment and a SACK of just [30,35). The first case fixes a missed delivery; the second credits bytes never reported delivered.

evidence.label: Exact PR head, same two packets

findings.text: On #16660, with no new ACKs, repeated application writes that put no data on the wire postponed the three-second retransmission past six seconds. An ACK one byte beyond SND.NXT caused a second probe 60 ms later. A quiet sender retransmitted at three seconds, and a duplicate ACK did not trigger a second probe.

In a separate stock sender test, ordinary TCP repeated the highest outstanding segment in its tail probe, but software segmentation repeated the first packet instead of the last. Sending just the tail on both exact and short final segments corrected the two traces.

Outside loss recovery, #15325 reports better receive behavior under small-segment pressure but still allocates one charged header per discarded payload. Test queue growth with the processing goroutine paused. #16180 needs a dual-stack wildcard bind, mapped-v4 connect, close, and IPv6-only port rebind case; the suspected reservation imbalance comes from source inspection. #15019 already has a regression and downstream confirmation.

evidence.label: Reproducible 5/5 Reno stall on the reported synthetic trace
